rationale: Improper input validation produces incorrect results when malformed input reaches business logic; cross-cutting security impact tracked via parent OWASP category.
Path traversal exposes files outside the intended directory to unauthorized actors.
Generic command injection alters program behavior by executing attacker-controlled commands.
OS command injection lets attackers modify or replace executed commands.
XSS injects attacker-controlled script into trusted output altering integrity of rendered content.
SQL injection lets attackers modify queries and underlying data.
LDAP injection alters directory queries and authentication/authorization decisions.
Code injection allows attacker-supplied code to execute changing program behavior.
Improper log neutralization permits log forging that breaks the audit trail.
Buffer boundary violations corrupt memory and alter program state.
Out-of-bounds read leaks memory contents to attackers.
Integer overflow produces incorrect arithmetic results that may also have security consequences.
Direct exposure of sensitive information to unauthorized actors.
Error messages disclose sensitive implementation or data to attackers.
Unprotected storage of credentials exposes them to anyone with filesystem read access.
Improper privilege management lets actors operate with privileges they should not have altering protected state.
Improper access control allows unauthorized access to resources.
Improper authorization permits access beyond the actor's intended permissions.
Improper authentication fails to prove the claimed identity of the actor.
Improper certificate validation undermines TLS-based identity proofs.
Missing authentication for critical function lets any actor invoke it without proving identity.
Improper restriction of excessive authentication attempts enables brute force against identity proofs.
Missing encryption of sensitive data exposes it in transit or at rest.
Cleartext transmission of sensitive information allows network observers to read it.

Hard-coded cryptographic keys are recoverable by anyone with artifact access, exposing whatever the key protects (cf. CWE-798); forged-proof (authenticity) impact is the signing-key subcase, secondary.
Broken or risky cryptographic algorithms fail to keep data confidential against modern adversaries.
Improper verification of cryptographic signature undermines authenticity guarantees.
CSRF causes the application to perform state-changing actions on behalf of the user without their intent.
Race condition leaves the system in inconsistent states under common concurrent operation.
Divide by zero raises an unhandled arithmetic exception that crashes the operation; wrong-result (functional) impact secondary.
Session fixation prevents actions from being uniquely traced to the original authenticated entity.
Uncontrolled resource consumption can render the system unavailable when the resource is exhausted.
Memory leaks waste resources over time.
Algorithmic complexity attacks force worst-case time behavior.
Use after free corrupts state by operating on freed memory.
Unrestricted file upload lets attackers place executable or active content within the system.
NULL pointer dereference crashes the process under faulty input.
Download of code without integrity check permits substitution of trusted code.
Trust boundary violation mixes trusted and untrusted data corrupting downstream decisions.
Deserialization of untrusted data lets attackers craft objects that alter program behavior.
Insufficiently protected credentials may be read by unauthorized actors.
Insertion of sensitive information into log file exposes it to anyone with log read access.
XML external entity reference can be coerced to read local files.
Authorization bypass through user-controlled key lets actors read other users' resources.
XPath injection alters XML query semantics.
Incorrect permission assignment for critical resource exposes it to unauthorized actors.
Improper handling of exceptional conditions degrades fault tolerance.
Allocation of resources without limits enables unbounded resource use.
Insufficient logging undermines the ability to prove actions occurred.
Out-of-bounds write corrupts memory altering program state.
Hard-coded credentials expose authentication material to anyone with source access.
Inclusion of functionality from untrusted control sphere imports attacker-controlled behavior.
Missing authorization lets unauthorized actors access protected resources.
Incorrect authorization grants access against policy.
Expression language injection alters template evaluation.
SSRF coerces the server into fetching attacker-chosen internal resources (metadata endpoints, internal services) whose responses reach the attacker; request-side state change (integrity) secondary.
Unmaintained third-party components cannot be patched or evolved safely; security impact (unfixed vulnerabilities) secondary.
Excessive code complexity degrades the ability to assess change impact.

Improper use of a validation framework lets malformed input reach business logic and produce incorrect results (as CWE-20); the weakness is developer misuse, not end-user error protection; security impact secondary.
Inefficient regular expression complexity (ReDoS) degrades response time.
